title: What City Am I In? City and Town From a Point
description: Identify the city or town for any point — What City Am I In? answers from administrative map data, by GPS or map click. Free.
summary_sentence: For example, standing in an unincorporated suburb, the honest answer may be 'no city — the county governs here', and this page gives that answer instead of borrowing the neighbouring city's name.
quick_answer: What City Am I In? identifies the city or town a point falls in from OpenStreetMap's administrative data. Use your location or click the map and read the city field — with the unincorporated truth preserved, because a borrowed name is worse than an honest county.

faq: The page says so when the point lies outside any municipality — county government is the honest answer there, and the county tools on this site take over.
Can I use the tool without sharing my precise location?
Yes — click any point instead of using GPS.
Why might a boundary or place name look different elsewhere?
Municipal boundaries change with annexations; postal and commercial sources draw their own 'city' notions. Administrative data is this page's standard.
Does MapBench store my browser location?
No — a GPS reading is used for the answer, not kept.
The record's classification and the place's legal status decide; the page reports the data's term for the point.
A point in a huge rural county with no towns?
The answer may be genuinely 'none nearby in the record' — the nearest-village and settlement tools frame the emptiness usefully.
Big cities' internal divisions are a finer layer — the District and Municipality finders read those records.
Does the postal city ever win?
For mail, always — addresses follow USPS logic. For governance, this page's answer wins. Knowing which question you asked is the skill.
Worldwide where boundary data exists — municipality concepts vary, and the record's own structure is reported.
